title: Forest Composition
text:
Purpose
NLCD splits forest into deciduous (41), evergreen (42), and mixed (43), but only at 30 m and from classified Landsat. The leaf-off orthoimagery shows evergreen foliage directly, at 1 ft. This page uses it to estimate what share of NLCD forest is evergreen and what share is deciduous, for each forest class and for each 1 km window along the transect.
Across the windows, NLCD maps 24.8 km² of forest. Of that, an estimated 29% is evergreen (95% interval 27%–31%), about 7.2 km², and 17.6 km² is deciduous.

title: Forest Composition
text:
Method
Sample. 48,517 random points in NLCD forest, at the same density everywhere (about 6000 in the most forested window). Each point gets its brightness-adjusted NDVI (ndvi_adj, see Holly candidates), averaged over its 3 × 3 ft neighbourhood. On this scale bare hardwood is near 0 at any brightness and evergreen foliage is higher.
Why not a threshold. The two kinds of pixel overlap. A cutoff that keeps false positives low misses most evergreen, and one that catches most evergreen also passes many deciduous pixels. In both cases the error depends on the true mix. For example, only 31% of points in NLCD evergreen forest exceed the crown threshold (1.7).
Mixture model. Instead, a two-component Gaussian mixture is fitted to all forest points pooled: one deciduous component and one evergreen component. The two components are then held fixed, and only the evergreen weight is re-estimated for each NLCD class and each window. That weight is the estimated share of forest area whose visible winter foliage is evergreen. The intervals come from 200 bootstrap replicates, each resampling points within windows and refitting the mixture, so they include uncertainty in the components themselves.

title: Forest Composition
text:
Notes

Leaf-off means “visible evergreen”. In winter, evergreen understory (holly, cedar, mountain laurel, evergreen shrubs) shows through bare hardwood canopy and counts as evergreen. These shares are therefore the evergreen part of what is seen from above in winter, and can be higher than the evergreen share of the leaf-on canopy. For holly this is useful: understory evergreens are part of what holly lives among.
Fixed components. The method assumes deciduous and evergreen pixels have the same ndvi_adj distribution everywhere. Differences in flight date, sun angle, or species mix along the transect would shift the components and bias some windows. The class check above suggests this is not a large effect overall, but it is not tested window by window.
NLCD forest boundaries. Forest is defined by the 30 m NLCD map, so the sample includes some gaps, edges, and roads inside forest cells, and leaves out trees outside mapped forest (street trees, yards). Those count toward neither share.
Small samples near the city. Windows with little forest have few points and wide intervals.
Not species. “Evergreen” lumps pine, cedar, holly, and evergreen shrubs; separating them would need texture or crown shape, or a leaf-on image to compare against.

title: Holly Candidates
text:
Purpose
American holly (Ilex opaca) is evergreen, so in leaf-off imagery (flown February to March 2025) its crowns stay green while the deciduous canopy around it is bare. This page builds the first step of a holly classification workflow:

Candidates from imagery (this page): find small, isolated evergreen crowns in non-developed areas.
Ground truth: visit candidate locations and record what is there (holly, sex if known, or the false-positive species).
Classification: train a supervised classifier on crown features (including NDVI and NIR) using the field labels, then map holly across the transect.

title: Holly Candidates
text:
Why NDVI
Healthy leaves treat red and near-infrared (NIR) light very differently. Chlorophyll absorbs most red light for photosynthesis, while the internal cell structure of a leaf (the spongy mesophyll) scatters and reflects most NIR light. Bare branches, dead or dormant grass, soil, and pavement show much less of this contrast. The normalized difference vegetation index captures it in one number:
\[
\text{NDVI} = \frac{\text{NIR} - \text{Red}}{\text{NIR} + \text{Red}}
\]
NDVI ranges from −1 to 1. Water is negative, soil, rock, and pavement sit near 0, and dense green foliage is typically above 0.6. Because it is a ratio, it is also less sensitive to illumination than a single band, so a shaded crown and a sunlit crown of the same tree give similar values.
This contrast is what makes leaf-off imagery useful for holly. In February and March the deciduous canopy is bare and has low NDVI, while evergreen foliage stays green and has high NDVI. Holly in the understory should stand out clearly against the bare hardwoods around it.
The RGB stand-in used for the first pass, the green leaf index (GLI), relies only on the small green reflectance peak of leaves in visible light. In this imagery GLI separates pine canopy (median about 0.03) from leaf-off hardwood (about −0.01) by only a narrow margin. It is also affected by shadows and by the imagery’s slight blue cast.

Separation in this imagery
To compare the indices and set thresholds, each was computed (3 × 3 px smoothed, as in crown extraction) at 60,000 random points in the study area and grouped by NLCD class (R/05b_ndvi_calibration.R). NLCD is a 30 m product, so these labels are noisy at 1 ft (a “deciduous” cell can contain a pine or a holly), which blurs every index.


Code
auc <- function(neg, pos) {
  r <- rank(c(neg, pos))
  (sum(r[length(neg) + seq_along(pos)]) - length(pos) * (length(pos) + 1) / 2) /
    (length(neg) * length(pos))
}

  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())









Plain NDVI rises steadily as pixels get darker. In leaf-off deciduous forest the median is about 0.2 for bright pixels and about 0.6 in shadow, the same as evergreen foliage: in shadow the red band falls nearly to zero while the NIR band stays high, lit by light scattered from the surrounding vegetation. A fixed NDVI threshold therefore picks up tree and building shadows. The first NDVI run did exactly this: its candidates were much darker than GLI’s, and many were shadows.
The brightness-adjusted NDVI compares each pixel with leaf-off deciduous forest at the same brightness:
\[
\text{NDVI}_\text{adj} = \frac{\text{NDVI} - \mu(b)}{\sigma(b)}
\]
where b is brightness and μ(b) and σ(b) are the mean and spread of NDVI in NLCD deciduous forest at that brightness (loess fits, saved in data/derived/ndvi_shadow_curve.csv). It is in units of deciduous-forest standard deviations: about 0 for bare hardwood at any brightness, positive for foliage greener than leaf-off forest. Dividing by σ(b) matters because NDVI is also noisier in shadow; subtracting the mean alone still let about 20% of shaded deciduous pixels through.
The crown threshold (1.7) is exceeded by about 5% of deciduous-forest pixels at every brightness, and the context threshold (1) by about 15%. The price is that evergreen foliage in deep shadow can no longer be told from shaded hardwood. That is a real limit of this imagery, not of the method: a shaded holly is invisible to both indices. Overall AUC drops a little because part of plain NDVI’s apparent separation came from evergreen canopy being darker than deciduous canopy, which is the shadow effect again.


Measuring the gain from NIR
Every crown carries GLI, plain NDVI, and the adjusted index (gli_mean, ndvi_mean, vi_mean) along with mean band values, including NIR. Once field labels exist, the comparison will use the same ground-truth set and the same spatially blocked cross-validation for two classifiers:

Visible only: crown features from RGB (GLI, colour, brightness, size, shape, isolation).
Visible + NIR: the same features plus NDVI and NIR reflectance.

The improvement will be reported as the change in precision (share of candidates that are holly), recall (share of holly found), and overall accuracy, along with how many candidates drop out of the field list.

title: Holly Candidates
text:
Approach
Each 12-inch tile is processed at full resolution:

Vegetation index (brightness-adjusted NDVI), smoothed with a 3 × 3 px mean.
Crowns: pixels with index > 1.7 are evergreen crown; connected groups of them are crown objects. Objects 6–30 ft across (equivalent-circle diameter) are kept with their features.
Isolation: the share of evergreen pixels (index > 1, a lower threshold) in the 70 ft neighbourhood of each crown. Holly in a leaf-off hardwood stand has a low share; a crown inside pine canopy has a high one.
Candidate rule: crown 10–20 ft across, evergreen share ≤ 0.25, and NLCD class not water or developed (11, 21, 22, 23, 24). Crowns cut by a tile edge are excluded from the field list.

Thresholds are calibrated on NLCD forest classes (see Separation in this imagery and Shadows).

Example
A 600 × 600 ft area 22.5 km along the transect: a pine stand (upper left) next to leaf-off hardwoods (lower right). Candidates are the isolated crowns in the hardwood stand; crowns inside the pine canopy are rejected as not isolated.

What changed.

GLI (RGB only) found crowns that look green in RGB, including green-tinted bark, litter, and moss with no near-infrared signal of live foliage.
Plain NDVI swapped that error for a worse one: its candidates are the darkest of the three runs (see brightness above), and the gallery for that run was dominated by tree and building shadows.
Adjusted NDVI candidates are mid-brightness crowns that are greener than leaf-off forest in both RGB (median GLI 0.04) and NIR. It shares more candidates with GLI (37% of GLI candidates) than with plain NDVI (19%), which is consistent with plain NDVI’s extra candidates being shadows. The gallery above shows sunlit green crowns in leaf-off hardwood, the pattern expected for understory evergreens.

The adjusted index yields the most candidates of the three, because its crown threshold admits 5% of deciduous-forest pixels (versus about 2% for the other two) to keep enough evergreen foliage above it once shadows no longer help. The rule can be tightened at render time (candidate_diam_ft, context_max in config.yml) if the field list is too long, but field results should guide that rather than the count alone.
Across all three runs candidate density rises from Richmond toward Pocahontas State Park, so the gradient itself does not depend on the index. Which list actually finds holly is a question for the field visits.

title: Holly Candidates
text:
Next steps

Sampling design: a stratified random sample of candidates per window (or per NLCD class), so the field effort covers the full gradient. To learn which index works, the visit list should also include a small random sample of crowns that only GLI or only plain NDVI flagged (their precision), and short searches around random points in non-developed land (holly the candidates missed, for recall). Recording what every visited crown actually is, holly or not, is what turns the visits into training data for the classifier.
Classifier: with field labels, fit a supervised model (e.g. random forest) on crown features, validated with spatially blocked cross-validation (hold out whole windows).
Threshold check: once field data exist, check the NDVI thresholds against crowns of known holly (the current values are calibrated on NLCD forest classes, not on holly).

title: Holly Candidates
text:
Notes

Expected false positives: other evergreens of similar size, such as eastern red cedar, young loblolly or Virginia pine, southern magnolia, and evergreen shrubs (privet, Elaeagnus, mountain laurel), plus green ground cover such as winter grass or English ivy on trunks.
What is missed: holly under evergreen canopy (hidden), crowns smaller than 10 ft, holly in developed areas (excluded by design), and crowns merged with neighbouring evergreens into one larger object.
Shadows: the imagery has long shadows in places. NDVI is a ratio, so it is less affected than GLI, but deep shadow lowers both bands to near the noise level and makes NDVI unreliable there.
Winter lawns: cool-season grass is green in February and March and has high NDVI. Lawns are mostly removed by the NLCD rule (developed classes) and by crown size and shape.

text:
Notes

Imagery source: VBMP 2025 12-inch orthoimagery (Sanborn Map Company, flown February to March 2025), distributed by the Virginia Geographic Information Network (VGIN). The MrSID versions are RGB only. The near-infrared band is only in the 4-band GeoTIFF deliverables, which share the MrSID tiles’ names and pixel grid exactly (same 5,000 × 5,000 px extent and origin, EPSG:2925). Their RGB bands are the uncompressed originals: compared with the MrSID-derived RGB they differ by about 5 digital numbers on average, with no bias (MrSID compression noise), so the 4-band tiles replace the MrSID set.
Tile layout: each 12-inch tile is 5,000 × 5,000 px at 1 ft, covering 5,000 × 5,000 ft. Tile names follow DO_S13_<section>_<quarter>.2025.
MrSID decoding (only needed with imagery_source: "rgb"): the MrSID GDAL driver only loads inside the QGIS application (macOS code-signing blocks it from the command line), so conversion runs in the QGIS Python console.
Mosaic edges: the VRT has no nodata value. Areas outside the tiles read as 0 in all bands; all such areas lie outside the study area.

This site documents spatial analyses components of this project using the 2025 Virginia Base Mapping Program (VBMP) 12-inch orthoimagery along a 25 km transect from industrial Richmond, Virginia (37.584817° N, 77.472433° W) to Pocahontas State Park (37.373768° N, 77.570813° W), buffered by 2 km on each side. title: Licensed to Ilex
text:
Framing

Urbanization is treated as a continuous gradient, not an urban-versus-rural comparison. The goal is to identify “phase shifts” from urban to peri-urban to secondary forest, with applied value for managing human-modified landscapes.
It builds directly on the dogwood work: about 60 maternal trees sampled from Richmond to Pocahontas State Park, with mating system parameters analyzed against spatial, impervious surface, and land cover gradients.
Holly is framed as an Anthropocene “winner,” like pigeons and rats, a species doing well in human landscapes that’s worth understanding for that reason.

title: Licensed to Ilex
text:
Questions

Sex ratios: Holly is dioecious, and the nursery trade sells grafted female clones. Urban areas may be female-biased, which could lower seed set through limited pollen.
Pollination: Little is known about who pollinates holly. The visitors appear to be mostly generalists. One hypothesis is that non-native urban pollinators compensate, so there’s no net effect on seed set.
Herbivory: The holly leaf miner and its parasitoids, including possible co-evolution along the gradient.
Leaf traits and physiology: Leaf toughness, LI-COR gas exchange, and water-use efficiency, linked to herbivore performance (modeled on the Costa Rica caterpillar study).
Fragmentation: Holly often grows on forest edges, so edge versus interior is a related axis.
Longer term: Reciprocal common gardens (Rice Rivers Center and an urban site near the Science Museum), and range-wide phylogeography, including high-elevation Appalachian populations.

title: Licensed to Ilex
text:
Approach

Start with low-cost observational data:

Map and sex trees after leaf drop,
Collect seeds from mother trees through December (freezer storage),
Photograph leaves on target trees for herbivory,
Rear leaf miners for parasitoids,
Run pollinator counts in April–June.
Germination tests, seed abortion, etc. ~ (landscape location).

Recruit undergraduates by pitching to targeted courses: GIS/cartography for spatial work, ecology for herbivory & pollinators, and evolution for co-evolution.
Formats include independent study, the new zero-credit research course, and a possible fall capstone or seminar that produces the literature review.
An NSF submission is planned.

Evergreen cover follows the urban-to-forest gradient only loosely. It is lowest in downtown Richmond (about 7–9% at km 0–2), sits between about 12% and 22% through most of the transect, and peaks at 43% at km 21–22, where pine stands are common. In the developed windows part of the signal is green winter lawn and street trees rather than evergreen canopy; the adjusted index is calibrated on forest, so it is least reliable on bright urban surfaces.
Within forest the evergreen share does not follow the urban gradient. The small forest patches near km 9–11 are pine-rich (41–46% evergreen), the forests at km 12–20 are mostly deciduous (18–28%), km 21–22 is pine-rich again (54%), and km 23–24 is hardwood-dominated (about 19%). The amount of forest (NLCD) and its composition (NDVI) change at different places along the transect. That matters for holly: an isolated evergreen crown is easiest to see, and most likely to be holly, in deciduous forest. Windows 1–4 have no NLCD forest, so they have no forest-only value.

title: Urban to Forest Gradient
text:
Notes

Data: Annual NLCD Collection 1, 2025 land cover (LndCov) and fractional impervious surface (FctImp), read for the AOI bounding box from the USGS web coverage service (https://dmsdata.cr.usgs.gov/geoserver). No resampling or reprojection of the rasters.
Developed combines NLCD classes 22–24 (low, medium, high intensity). Developed open space (21) is mostly lawns, parks, and road verges and is kept separate. Forest is classes 41–43; wetland is 90 and 95.
NDVI: computed at full 1 ft resolution from the 4-band VBMP tiles and summarized into 10 ft cells (mean NDVI and share of pixels above the evergreen threshold) before the window summaries. NLCD is resampled to the 10 ft grid (nearest neighbour) only to mask water and select forest. The NIR band is not radiometrically calibrated, so NDVI values are relative to this imagery, and leaf-off timing means NDVI says little about deciduous canopy.
Windows are not replicated samples. Adjacent windows are spatially autocorrelated, so the curves describe the gradient but should not be treated as 25 independent observations.
The 4 km width averages across very different ground on either side of the line (e.g. the James River crossing near 5–7 km). A narrower center band would test how much that matters.

title: Focal Trees
text:
Purpose
Field work needs a fixed set of focal trees: holly that will be mapped, sexed, and followed for seed set, herbivory, and pollinators. This page picks 100 of them from the holly candidates, plus ranked alternates, so that:

they are spread evenly across the urbanization gradient, from forest to downtown;
within each part of the gradient they span landscape heterogeneity (mixed versus uniform surroundings) and distance along the transect;
no two listed trees are closer than 100 m, to reduce the chance of sampling parent–offspring pairs or sibships from the same seed shadow.









Step
Script
Output




10. Landscape metrics, indices, selection
R/08_focal_trees.R
data/derived/landscape_30m.tif, focal_bins.csv, focal_trees.{gpkg,csv,gpx}









ImportantCandidates, not confirmed holly



These are crowns that the imagery flags as small, isolated evergreens. Some will be other species, especially on developed land (magnolia, cedar, boxwood, other ornamentals). Each bin therefore has 10 ranked alternates. If a primary is not holly, or cannot be accessed, use the next alternate in the same bin. All 200 listed trees respect the spacing rule, so any substitution keeps it.

title: Focal Trees
text:
Pool
The pool is every crown that passes the size (10–20 ft) and isolation (evergreen share ≤ 0.25) parts of the candidate rule, not cut by a tile edge. Unlike the holly candidate list, developed land is included: without it the urban end of the transect (km 0–4) has almost no candidates. Only open water is excluded. Pool size: 30,508 crowns.

title: Focal Trees
text:
Landscape context
Each crown is described by its surroundings within 500 m, computed on the native 30 m Annual NLCD grid (2025):







Metric
Meaning




imperv_mean
mean fractional impervious surface (%)


imperv_sd
standard deviation of impervious surface among cells: patchiness of development


forest_pct, developed_pct
share of forest (41–43) and developed (21–24) cover


shdi
Shannon diversity of grouped land cover (developed, developed open, forest, wetland, water, …)


shei
Shannon evenness: diversity relative to its maximum for the classes present (0 = one class, 1 = all equal)


edge_density
metres of boundary between grouped cover types per hectare



Two indices are used:

Urbanization index = imperv_mean. A PCA of all metrics was tried first, but its first axis saturated at the urban end: forest and developed shares reach 0% and 100% well before the urban core, so it could not separate suburbs from downtown. Impervious surface keeps rising all the way to the core.
Heterogeneity index = first principal component of shdi, shei, edge_density, imperv_sd across all 30 m cells in the study area (70% of their variance). Higher values mean more mixed, more evenly divided, more fragmented surroundings.

The two indices therefore describe different things, and a design that balanced on land-cover fractions alone would sample the peri-urban mix without controlling for it.

text:
Notes

Spacing. 100 m is a working choice. Holly fruit is bird-dispersed, and most seeds of bird-dispersed trees fall within a few hundred metres of the parent, so trees 100 m apart can still be related. A genetic check (e.g. a kinship estimate from markers) on the final set would show how much residual relatedness remains. Increase min_spacing_m in config.yml and rerun R/08_focal_trees.R (about 30 s) to tighten it.
Scale. Landscape context uses a 500 m radius, a common scale for urban landscape effects on plants and their insects. Pollinator and leaf-miner responses may work at other scales; the metrics can be recomputed at several radii for analysis without changing the tree list.
Access. Urban bins fall largely on private land (yards, institutional grounds). Expect more substitutions there, from both access and ornamental look-alikes.
NLCD limits. Context comes from 30 m NLCD, so small features (a single street tree’s yard, a narrow riparian strip) are blurred. Neighbourhoods near the edge of the NLCD extract are truncated.
